title: Primes
summary: Set ENIAC hunting for prime numbers.

text.headline: Count up by 2
text.body: Any even number splits into 2 equal groups, so ENIAC tests only odd numbers: 3, 5, 7... It must step up by 2 each time. Tap the glowing dial on the Constant Transmitter and choose 2.
text.more: The Constant Transmitter has two sets of dials. J holds the number to start from, here 1. K holds the step, here 2. ENIAC adds the step to its test number again and again.
text.done: Now ENIAC will step up by 2 each time.

hints.wrongSwitch: That is a different dial. Try the glowing one.
hints.wrongValue: We want to step by 2. Pick 2.

text.headline: Let the checker call out
text.body: Accumulator 1 is the groups-of-3 checker. When a number splits into equal groups of 3, it sends a signal: 'fits!' Tap the 12-out jack on Accumulator 1. Then tap program trunk 1-7.
text.more: Each checker tries one group size. The groups-of-3 checker calls out for 9, 15, 21, and so on. We have wired 13 more checkers just like this one, for groups of 5, 7, 11, and on up to 47.

hints.wrongFrom: That jack is for a different signal. Look for 12, out.

text.headline: Let the conductor listen
text.body: The Master Programmer is ENIAC's conductor. It decides what happens next. Tap program trunk 1-7. Then tap the A-DI jack on the Master Programmer, so it can hear every 'fits!'.
text.more: If any checker calls out 'fits!', the conductor skips the card. If none do, the number will not split into equal groups at all. The real Master Programmer had ten steppers, a bit like a music box with pins.
text.done: The conductor can now hear the checkers.

hints.wrongTo: That jack is for a different job. Look for A, DI.

text.headline: Punch a card for every prime
text.body: If no group size fits, the number is prime. The conductor then sends a signal on program trunk 1-9. Tap trunk 1-9. Then tap the PI jack on the Initiating Unit. That starts the card punch.
text.more: A card punch makes holes in a card, one number per card. It could punch about 100 cards a minute. Our simulator copies that pace, so it cannot hurry any faster.
text.done: Now every prime will get a punched card.

hints.wrongTo: That jack starts something else. We want the card punch.

text.headline: Go on to the next number
text.body: When a card is punched, ENIAC moves on. The punch sends a done signal. Tap the PO jack on the Initiating Unit. Then tap program trunk 1-4, which starts the next number.
text.more: A loop is when the end of a job starts the job again. ENIAC runs this one about 1,400 times, from 3 up to 2,801, and then stops.
text.done: Punch, then next number. That loop is the whole program!

byTarget.i.pi: That is the punch start. We want the one that says done: PO.

briefing.headline: What is a prime?
briefing.body: Can you share 12 cookies evenly? Yes: 3 groups of 4. Now try 7. There is always one left over. Numbers that won't split into equal groups are prime: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11…
briefing.more: For parents: a prime is a number above 1 that divides evenly only by 1 and itself. Over a July 1946 holiday weekend, D. H. Lehmer used ENIAC to study primes. Brian Stuart's program follows De Mol and Bullynck's reconstruction.

plan.headline: Here is the trick
plan.body: ENIAC tests one number at a time. It tries to split it into groups of 3, 5, 7, and more, all at once. If any group size works, it's out. If none work, it's prime!
plan.more: ENIAC skips even numbers, which always split into 2 equal groups. It needs only 14 group sizes, 3 up to 47. A number below 2,809 (53 x 53) that is not prime always splits into equal groups of 47 or fewer. That is why this search stops at 2,801. Crossing out multiples is an old idea called a sieve.
plan.math: 9 = 3 groups of 3 -> out   11: no equal groups -> prime

rest.headline: The rest is done for you
rest.body: Real ENIAC programmers placed hundreds of cables by hand. Setting up a new problem could take a day or more. We will place the last ones now: 264 cables and 285 switches, including 13 more group checkers.

before.headline: Press INIT
before.sub: INIT is the Initiating Pulse, ENIAC's GO button.

captions.text: ENIAC gives each checker its group size.
3 won't split into equal groups. Nothing fits, so ENIAC punched a card.
9 splits into 3 groups of 3, so no card.
Only primes get a card. Watch them pile up.

result.headline: ENIAC found the primes!
result.body: Every card is a prime: a number that won't split into equal groups. ENIAC tried groups of 3, 5, 7 and more on each odd number. Same machine as Squares, with different cables.
result.more: The old idea of crossing out multiples is called the sieve of Eratosthenes, after a Greek scholar. ENIAC did it with 14 counters instead of a pencil. Today, big primes help keep online messages secret.
result.takeaway: Same machine. Different cables. A different job.
result.takeawaySub: Changing the cables changed what ENIAC did.

live.waiting: ENIAC is counting primes: {n} of the first 100
live.pending: ENIAC is still working: {n} primes so far.
live.done: ENIAC has found them all: {n} primes, from 3 to 2,801.

credits: Brian L. Stuart, programs/sieve.e. After D. H. Lehmer's July 1946 runs, as reconstructed by L. De Mol and M. Bullynck.
